newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN to woo Zaire refugees with clockwork radios.
newsitem.headline: UN to woo Zaire refugees with clockwork radios.

text.p: Rwandan refugees stranded by war in eastern Zaire's remote tropical forests will soon be able to follow the course of fighting and learn of safe corridors with new clockwork radios to be distributed by the U.N. refugee agency.

With a twist of the wrist, the refugees will be able to surf the world's airwaves, find out whether the rebels are advancing or retreating or tune into the latest message from UNHCR chief Sadako Ogata in Geneva.

The distribution of radios will be a first for UNHCR, which sees information as a potential life-saver just like food, blankets and plastic sheeting, its head of mass information, Joel Boutroue, said.

"The radios will give refugees unhindered access to information. For us, this is the first step to getting independent information to refugees so they can make up their own minds," Boutroue told Reuters on Wednesday.
The Western world may be suffering from an information glut, but for millions of illiterate people in African society, with its oral traditions, radio is the only medium for information.
The beauty of the clockwork radio, invented by Briton Trevor Baylis, is that it gives 40 minutes' playing time on short wave, medium wave and FM from 30 seconds' winding.
Radio is power in Africa and international news broadcasts can often be the only source of independent information.
In Liberia, warlord Charles Taylor often reached his people by giving interviews to the BBC on a satellite phone.
In Rwanda, radio was a source of evil during 1994's ethnic frenzy when extremist broadcasts exhorted Hutus to kill Tutsis.
The windup radio could be a godsend to communications in eastern Zaire as concern grows about the safety of 400,000 Hutus trapped amid fighting between rebels and Zairean troops.
Aid agencies say up to 200 refugees a week are dying from disease and hunger. More than 40,000 are on the run and agencies fear the fluid military situation may force many more to flee.
Boutroue said 1,000 clockwork radios donated by Britain, one for every five refugee families, would be sent to the region soon.

Groups of Rwandan Hutus gathered around a single short-wave radio listening to the news is a common sight in remote refugee settlements where children ride wooden bikes and modern communications, roads or telephones do not exist.

UNHCR says the flow of information to the refugees is controlled by Hutu soldiers and militiamen who committed 1994's genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda and are feeding fellow refugees with propaganda and fear-mongering.

UNHCR is hoping to work with a local radio station in east Zaire's regional hub of Kisangani to boost broadcasts for refugees on health, separated families, independent news, conditions of return inside Rwanda and interviews.

It is also financing extended daily BBC broadcasts to the troubled Great Lakes region in a mixture of the Kinyarwanda and Kirundi languages -- mutually understandable and spoken by an estimated 80 percent of Rwandans and Burundians.
Boutroue said the BBC World Service was the most popular and most listened to radio station in the region.

The clockwork radio, produced by South African company BayGen Power with financing from the British Overseas Development Administration (ODA), won the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) television design award in 1996.
The windup radios have already gone on sale in upmarket London stores like Harrods and have been a hit. This is the first time they will be used by a humanitarian agency.

In the age of digital technology, Microsoft Windows and Internet, Boutroue believes this simple windup radio with a tough plastic case and a flip-out winder to power its generator could revolutionise UNHCR's information campaigns for refugees.
"Refugees have few radios, even fewer batteries," he said.

"This is a battle for control of information. It is a fairly new thinking at the UNHCR. The use of radio to inform refugees has great potential as a means of preventing conflict and building ethnic harmony. Information is very important."
